Draw it on the board. Anxiety is a forecast; avoiding means it never gets checked. Reassurance works like leaving: relief, and the prediction stays untested.

Slide 11 · Notes

Your body can’t stay at peak alarm for long. When you stay, the feeling crests and settles, and your brain collects new evidence: I handled that.

Slide 12 · Notes

Peaks within minutes: pounding heart, short breath, dizziness. Frightening, and it passes. Never had chest pain checked? See a doctor once. Practice the breath together for one minute.

Therapists call this exposure. It works mainly by proving the prediction wrong, so you don’t have to feel calm for it to count. Bigger fears are worth doing with a counselor.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain how avoidance teaches anxiety to ring louder, describe a panic attack as an alarm with no fire that peaks and passes, and run one small experiment that tests an anxious prediction. Nobody is asked to name their own fears.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 8 minFour myths, one per slide
  2. 5 minThe avoidance loop, and stay so it settles
  3. 5 minPanic: the alarm with no fire, and the breath
  4. 5 minCommon false alarms: turn and talk, share out
  5. 5 minRun the experiment, and the excited guess
  6. 8 minToast or fire? Theo, Sofia, Nate
  7. 5 minBuild a ladder
  8. 4 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Two myths, the avoidance loop, panic, toast or fire with two stories, and the ladder.

Before you teach
Assume someone in the room has panic attacks.

About 1 in 3 teens meets criteria for an anxiety disorder by 18. Never ask students to name their own fears or share a ladder. If someone volunteers, keep it brief and thank them. Say at the start and the end that a counselor is available afterward.

If a student panics during class.

Stay calm and quiet, and keep the room's attention off them. Offer a choice: step into the hall with you or another adult, or stay put. Speak slowly. Breathe with them, in for 4, out for 6. Say it will peak and pass in a few minutes. Don't crowd them, touch them without asking, or tell them to calm down. Afterward, let them rejoin without comment.

When to bring in the nurse.

Send them to the nurse, with an escort, if it's the first time you've seen it, if they mention chest pain, fainting, or a health condition like asthma or diabetes, or if you aren't sure it's panic. The nurse can rule out a medical cause. Call 911 if a student passes out, can't breathe, or seems confused.

When to bring in a counselor.

Tell a counselor the same day after any panic episode in class. Also refer if a student is missing classes, practices or friends because of anxiety, is using vapes, weed, alcohol or pills to cope, or says they feel hopeless. Disclosures go to a counselor. No screening questions in class.

Exposure is the student's choice.

This lesson teaches the idea. Don't push anyone into a feared situation to practice, and don't cold-call an anxious student to prove a point. Bigger fears belong with a counselor or therapist. Existing accommodations stay in place.

Burnt toast is the target. Real danger still counts.

Some fears are accurate. Bullying, an unsafe home, or a friend in medical trouble needs a real response. If the voting surfaces something like that, take it seriously and follow up with a counselor.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Not every family calls it anxiety.

Some say stress, nerves, or overthinking. In some homes it shows up as stomachaches or headaches and gets treated as a body problem. Some lean on faith, family or community. Any of those can sit alongside these tools. Ask what words students' own families use, privately.

Some fears are realistic.

Students who face racism, worry about a family member's immigration status, or have been targeted for who they are may carry fears that match real risk. Don't label those false alarms. Keep the burnt-toast examples to everyday things like calls, tryouts and group chats.

LGBTQ+ students and being seen.

Social anxiety can be tied to whether a student is out, and to whom. Never use coming out as an exposure example. For any student who needs support beyond school hours, The Trevor Project (1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678) sits alongside 988.

Neurodivergent and disabled students.

Autistic students and students with sensory or processing differences may avoid noise, crowds or eye contact for reasons that aren't anxiety. Don't treat eye contact, speaking up, or sitting still as signs of being okay. Accommodations aren't avoidance.

"Coaching, not rescue" works with any adult.

The parent research applies to whoever raises the student: one parent, two, a grandparent, foster or kinship caregivers, an older sibling. Say "the adults in your life." Some students have no adult at home to coach them; a counselor or coach can fill that role.

Language, money and phone calls.

Some students already make calls for their family, sometimes in a second language. That counts as hard work they've done. Help is free at school: a counselor and the nurse. Outside school, community clinics offer sliding-scale care and interpreters.

What the research says

In a national survey of more than 10,000 U.S. teens, about 1 in 3 met criteria for an anxiety disorder at some point by age 18.

Merikangas et al., Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 2010

Exposure works mainly through expectation violation: you predict something bad, it doesn't happen, and the brain stores a new memory that competes with the fear. Feeling calm isn't required.

Craske et al., Behaviour Research and Therapy, 2014 (UCLA)

In a trial with kids ages 7 to 14, coaching parents to stop accommodating anxiety, while staying warm and supportive, worked as well as therapy with the child directly.

Lebowitz et al., 2020

In a major U.S. trial with ages 7 to 17, about 60% improved with 12 weeks of CBT, 55% with sertraline, and 81% with both, compared with 24% on placebo.

Walkup et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2008

People who said "I am excited" before karaoke, public speaking, or a math test did better than people who tried to calm down.

Brooks, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014

A panic attack is a surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes: pounding heart, short breath, dizziness, shaking, a sense of doom. Anyone who has never had symptoms like chest pain checked should see a doctor once.
